summary.text: For composite \(n=2^e m\), if \(m>1\) a proper odd prime \(p\mid n\) is shown—using Fermat and lifting-the-exponent estimates on the selected factors \(2^{(p-1)j}-1\)—to divide \(a(n-1)\), contradicting the hypothesis since \(p\nmid2^{n-2}\); if \(m=1\), the calculation \(v_2(a(2^e-1))=e-1\) likewise rules out divisibility by \(2^e\). For prime \(p\), exact divisibility of the defining numerator by the factorial, followed by reduction modulo \(p\) and Wilson’s theorem, gives \(\prod_{1\le k<p-1}(2^k-1)=1\); thus no positive exponent below \(p-1\) sends \(2\) to \(1\), while Fermat’s theorem does at exponent \(p-1\), proving that \(2\) is primitive.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 P_m:=\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1),\qquad N_m:=2^{m-1}P_m.
\]
Thus, for every positive integer \(m\),
\[
 a(m)=\frac{N_m}{m!}.
\]
We first justify that this quotient is an integer and establish the divisibility facts that will be needed later.

Throughout the proof, for a prime \(q\) and a nonzero positive integer \(x\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of \(x\).

### 1. Integrality of the formula for \(a(m)\)

We claim that
\[
 m!\mid N_m
 \tag{1}
\]
for every positive integer \(m\).

Fix a prime \(q\). A standard form of Legendre's formula, expressed in terms of the base-\(q\) digits of \(m\), is
\[
 (q-1)v_q(m!)=m-s_q(m),
 \tag{2}
\]
where \(s_q(m)\) is the sum of the base-\(q\) digits of \(m\). Since \(m>0\), its base-\(q\) expansion is nonempty and has at least one nonzero digit, so \(s_q(m)\geq 1\). Consequently,
\[
 v_q(m!)\leq \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{q-1}\right\rfloor.
 \tag{3}
\]

If \(q=2\), (3) gives \(v_2(m!)\leq m-1\), while \(N_m\) visibly contains the factor \(2^{m-1}\). Hence \(v_2(m!)\leq v_2(N_m)\).

Now suppose that \(q\) is odd, and put
\[
 Q=\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{q-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
For each \(j=1,\dots,Q\), the integer \((q-1)j\) lies between \(1\) and \(m-1\). Fermat's theorem gives
\[
 2^{q-1}\equiv 1\pmod q,
\]
because \(q\nmid 2\). Raising this congruence to the \(j\)-th power yields
\[
 q\mid 2^{(q-1)j}-1.
\]
Thus the \(Q\) distinct factors of \(P_m\) indexed by \((q-1),2(q-1),\dots,Q(q-1)\) each contribute at least one factor of \(q\). Therefore
\[
 v_q(P_m)\geq Q\geq v_q(m!),
\]
and hence also \(v_q(N_m)\geq v_q(m!)\).

This holds for every prime \(q\), proving (1). In particular, the displayed quotient defining \(a(m)\) is exact, and
\[
 m!\,a(m)=N_m.
 \tag{4}
\]

### 2. An odd proper prime divisor of \(n\) divides \(a(n-1)\)

We next prove the key composite-number lemma.

**Lemma.** Let \(n>2\), and let \(p\) be an odd prime such that \(p\mid n\) and \(p<n\). Then
\[
 p\mid a(n-1).
 \tag{5}
\]

Write
\[
 n=pr.

the condition \(p<n\) implies \(r\geq2\). Set \(M=n-1=pr-1\). We shall compare the \(p\)-adic valuations of \(P_M\) and \(M!\).

For every \(j=1,\dots,r\), consider the exponent
\[
 k_j=(p-1)j.
\]
It is positive, and
\[
 k_j\leq (p-1)r=pr-r<pr-1=M

tbecause \(r\geq2\). Hence all the factors
\[
 2^{(p-1)j}-1\qquad(1\leq j\leq r)
\]
occur among the factors making up \(P_M=\prod_{1\leq k<M}(2^k-1)\).

We use the following standard lifting-the-exponent consequence. If \(p\) is odd, \(p\mid X-1\), and \(p\nmid X\), then for every positive \(j\),
\[
 v_p(X^j-1)=v_p(X-1)+v_p(j).
 \tag{6}
\]
Take \(X=2^{p-1}\). Fermat's theorem gives \(p\mid X-1\), while clearly \(p\nmid X\). Thus (6) gives
\[
 v_p\bigl(2^{(p-1)j}-1\bigr)
 =v_p(2^{p-1}-1)+v_p(j)
 \geq 1+v_p(j).
 \tag{7}
\]
Summing (7) for \(j=1,\dots,r\), and using additivity of valuations on products, gives
\[
 v_p(P_M)
 \geq r+\sum_{j=1}^r v_p(j)
 =r+v_p(r!).
 \tag{8}
\]
In particular, since \((r-1)!\mid r!\),
\[
 v_p(P_M)\geq r+v_p((r-1)!).
 \tag{9}
\]

On the other hand,
\[
 M=pr-1=p(r-1)+(p-1).

the integers strictly between \(p(r-1)\) and \(p(r-1)+(p-1)\) are not divisible by \(p\). Therefore appending these last \(p-1\) factors to \((p(r-1))!\) does not change its \(p\)-adic valuation:
\[
 v_p(M!)=v_p((p(r-1))!).
 \tag{10}
\]
The factorial recurrence
\[
 v_p((ps)!)=v_p(s!)+s
 \tag{11}
\]
follows immediately from Legendre's formula
\(v_p(t!)=\sum_{i\geq1}\lfloor t/p^i\rfloor\): substituting \(t=ps\), the first term is \(s\), and the remaining terms sum to \(v_p(s!)\). Applying (11) with \(s=r-1\), we obtain
\[
 v_p(M!)=v_p((r-1)!)+(r-1).
 \tag{12}
\]
Comparing (9) and (12),
\[
 v_p(P_M)\geq v_p(M!)+1.
 \tag{13}
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, the factor \(2^{M-1}\) adds no negative issue—in fact it has \(p\)-adic valuation zero—and hence
\[
 v_p(N_M)\geq v_p(M!)+1.
\]
By the exact divisibility (4),
\[
 v_p(a(M))=v_p(N_M)-v_p(M!)\geq1.
\]
Thus \(p\mid a(M)=a(n-1)\), proving the lemma.

An immediate consequence is that if an odd prime \(p\) is a proper divisor of \(n>2\), then
\[
 n\nmid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
 \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, if \(n\) divided that sum, then so would \(p\). The lemma says that \(p\mid a(n-1)\), so subtraction would give \(p\mid2^{n-2}\). Since \(p\) is prime, this would imply \(p\mid2\), impossible for an odd prime.

### 3. Powers of two do not satisfy the divisibility

It remains to rule out composite numbers having no odd prime divisor, namely powers of two.

Suppose
\[
 n=2^e,
 \qquad e\geq2.

the lower bound on \(e\) is automatic if \(n>2\). Put \(M=2^e-1=n-1\). Every factor \(2^k-1\) in \(P_M\) is odd, so
\[
 v_2(P_M)=0.

tConsequently,
\[
 v_2(N_M)=v_2(2^{M-1})=M-1=2^e-2.
 \tag{15}
\]

Legendre's formula gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_2((2^e-1)!)
 &=\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{2^e-1}{2^i}\right\rfloor\\
 &=\sum_{i=1}^{e-1}(2^{e-i}-1)\\
 &=(2^e-2)-(e-1)\\
 &=2^e-1-e.
\end{aligned}
 \tag{16}
\]
Using (4), (15), and (16), we obtain the exact valuation
\[
 v_2(a(2^e-1))=(2^e-2)-(2^e-1-e)=e-1.
 \tag{17}
\]

For \(e\geq2\), one has
\[
 e+2\leq2^e.
 \tag{18}
\]
This is equality at \(e=2\), and the inequality is preserved when \(e\) is increased by one because the right side doubles. Hence \(e\leq2^e-2=n-2\), and therefore
\[
 2^e\mid2^{2^e-2}=2^{n-2}.
 \tag{19}
\]
If \(n=2^e\) divided \(a(n-1)+2^{n-2}\), then (19) would imply that \(2^e\mid a(n-1)\). That would require \(v_2(a(n-1))\geq e\), contrary to (17), which says that this valuation is only \(e-1\). Thus no power of two greater than \(2\) satisfies the required divisibility.

### 4. The divisibility hypothesis forces \(n\) to be prime

Now let \(n>2\) and assume
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
 \tag{20}
\]
We prove that \(n\) is prime.

Suppose instead that \(n\) is composite. Write
\[
 n=2^e m,

twhere \(m\) is odd. If \(m=1\), then \(n=2^e\). Since \(n>2\), we have \(e\geq2\), and Section 3 contradicts (20).

If \(m>1\), choose a prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(p\neq2\), so \(p\) is odd. Also \(p\mid n\). Finally, \(p<n\): if \(p=n\), then \(n\) itself would be prime, contrary to the supposition that it is composite. Thus \(p\) is an odd proper prime divisor of \(n\), and (14) again contradicts (20).

Both alternatives are impossible. Therefore \(n\) is prime. Since \(n>2\), it is an odd prime.

### 5. The prime case forces \(2\) to be a primitive root

Write \(p=n\), now known to be an odd prime. Work modulo \(p\), and define
\[
 R:=\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(2^k-1)\pmod p.
 \tag{21}
\]
We will prove that
\[
 R\equiv1\pmod p.
 \tag{22}
\]

Apply the sequence formula with \(m=p-1\). Since the quotient is exact,
\[
 a(p-1)=\frac{2^{p-2}P_{p-1}}{(p-1)!},

twhere \(P_{p-1}=\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(2^k-1)\), whose residue is \(R\). The denominator \((p-1)!\) is nonzero modulo \(p\), because none of its factors is divisible by \(p\). Thus division by it is legitimate in the field \(\mathbb F_p\), and the hypothesis (20) becomes
\[
 \frac{2^{p-2}R}{(p-1)!}+2^{p-2}=0
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.
 \tag{23}
\]
Multiplying by \((p-1)!\) and factoring gives
\[
 2^{p-2}\bigl(R+(p-1)!\bigr)=0.
 \tag{24}
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(2\not\equiv0\pmod p\), so \(2^{p-2}\neq0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). We may therefore cancel it from (24), obtaining
\[
 R+(p-1)!=0.
 \tag{25}
\]
Wilson's theorem states that for a prime \(p\),
\[
 (p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p.
\]
Substituting this into (25) gives precisely (22): \(R\equiv1\pmod p\).

In particular, \(R\) is nonzero modulo \(p\). A product in the field \(\mathbb F_p\) is nonzero only if each of its factors is nonzero. Hence, for every integer \(k\) with
\[
 1\leq k\leq p-2,

twe have
\[
 2^k-1\not\equiv0\pmod p,

tor equivalently,
\[
 2^k\not\equiv1\pmod p.
 \tag{26}
\]
On the other hand, Fermat's theorem gives
\[
 2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p.
 \tag{27}
\]
Thus no positive exponent smaller than \(p-1\) sends \(2\) to \(1\), while the exponent \(p-1\) does. The multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is therefore exactly \(p-1\).

Finally, for prime \(p\), Euler's totient satisfies \(\varphi(p)=p-1\). Hence \(2\) has order \(\varphi(p)\) in the multiplicative group modulo \(p\), which is exactly to say that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(p=n\).

We have proved both conclusions: \(n\) is prime, and \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).
